title: Why picking 33 loses this number game
description:
Everyone picks a number from 0 to 100, and the winner is closest to two thirds of the average. If picks were random the average would be 50, so 33 looks smart; but if everyone thinks that, the target is 22, then 15, then 10, all the way down to 0, the only answer that survives perfect logic. Real people stop after one or two steps: when the Danish newspaper Politiken ran the game in 2005 with 19,196 readers, the winning number was 21.6. The best pick is one step smarter than the crowd, not the smartest one.

Numbers checked in code (the 2/3 chain 33, 22, 15, 10 and 100,000 simulated crowds of level-k players). Sources: Wikipedia, Guess 2/3 of the average (Politiken, Nagel 1995).

facts_checked: Chain from random picks (average 50): 33.3, 22.2, 14.8, 9.9, 6.6 ... -> 0, the unique Nash equilibrium (verify.py; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guess_2/3_of_the_average)
Politiken (Denmark) 2005: 19,196 participants, winning number 21.6 (Wikipedia footnote citing Politiken 22 Sep 2005; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guess_2/3_of_the_average)
Real players reason about one or two levels (Nagel 1995, first-round average ~36) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guess_2/3_of_the_average)
Simulation: 100,000 crowds of 1,000 level-k players; 33 and 0 never closest, mean winning number 20.8 (verify.py)
